newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: OAU urges closer ties for human rights protection. [CORRECTED 16:15 GMT]
newsitem.headline: OAU urges closer ties for human rights protection. [CORRECTED 16:15 GMT]

text.p: The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) chief (corrects from Chairman) Salim Ahmed Salim on Monday called for a partnership of governments and private groups for better monitoring and protection of human rights on the continent.

"We need to build a partnership that brings together governments, individuals, and non-governmental organisations to observe, promote and protect human rights in our countries," Salim, OAU Secretary-General, told a conference.

"We must strive to establish creative joint ventures between non-governmental organisations, the private sector and governments so that working together, we can ensure the creation of popular based political processes..."
"Governments must see NGOs as natural allies in the search for a solution to the many problems confronting our continent," Salim added.
Salim spoke at the opening of the 20th session of OAU's African Commission on Human and People's Rights (ACHPR) meeting in the Indian Ocean island of Mauritius.

The 10-day meeting will adopt a five-year action plan which will shape out the ACHPR strategy in 1997-2002. Reports on human rights in the Indian Ocean islands of Seychelles, Comoros and Mauritius, and Uganda will be presented at the meeting.

Salim said better human rights protection could be achieved by promoting greater awareness in universities, schools and research agencies, empowering the ACHPR with more cash, creating closer links with grass roots organisations and civil societies and launching an African Court of Human and Peoples' Rights.
"It is important for the Commission to put in place measures to sensitize the public on principles and objectives enshrined in the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights," he said.
The meeting takes place against a backdrop of human rights violations in a number of African countries.

"Without any doubt, there has been improvements in the issue of human rights these last 10 years, but we must not rejoice too quickly, as today we still see numerous dark patches on the African human rights map," said International Commission of Jurists Secretary General Adama Dieng.
Dieng made reference to Burundi, Liberia, Zaire, Somalia, Nigeria and Sudan as areas where human rights were trampled on.
"Unfortunately, there is still a lot to do. Indeed, between what states promise and do, there is a gap which is often very wide..." Dieng added.
